texts.preamble: Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Sh. Murari Lal Mittal on 15 November, 2016 In The Court Of Sh. Ashu Garg, Addl. Chief Metropolitan Magistrate - Ii (New Delhi), Patiala House Courts, New Delhi
texts.facts: The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused persons have violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules. The accused no. 1 is stated to be the vendor-cum-proprietor of M/s. Bajrang Traders, from where Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Sh. Murari Lal Mittal on 15 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/163290650/ 1 the food article, that is, 'Vansapati' was lifted for sampling. Accused no. 2 (since discharged) is stated to be the supplier and manufacturing company, of which accused no. 3 is the nominee. 2. As per the complaint, on 09.08.2002, the food officials consisting of Food Inspectors (FI) Ranjeet Singh and S. B. Sharma under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. S. C. Tyagi reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s. Bajrang Traders, at 17/133, Geeta Colony, Delhi, where the accused no. 1 was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption. The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Vanaspati (Ladla) from the vendor as lying in sealed polythene pouches of 500 ml (448 grams) each, to which he agreed. A sample of three such pouches was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules. Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama, etc. The price of sample was paid to the vendor. Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA. Vide report dated 28.08.2002, the PA found the sample to be not conforming to the standards because it gave negative baudoiun test for presence of sesame oil. Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI. It was revealed that the accused no. 1 vendor had purchased the commodity from accused no. 2 company, of which accused no. 3 was the nominee. After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA. The complaint was then filed in the court on 13.01.2003 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act. 3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned vide order dated 13.01.2003. The accused persons appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising the right to get the second counterpart of the sample to be analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL). The application was allowed and a counterpart was sent for analysis to CFL. The CFL examined the sample and its Director gave Certificate dated 17.03.2003, opining the sample to be not conforming to the PFA Rues due to presence of free fatty acids and melting point more than the prescribed maximum limits. It also opined that the sample was misbranded due to violation od Rule 42(zzz)(17) of PFA Rules. 4. At this stage, it is pertinent to note that an application had been moved on behalf of the accused no. 2 company for dropping of the proceedings. This application was allowed vide order dated 11.02.2004 and the proceedings were stopped against the accused no. 2 company. Despite that, strangely, the accused no. 3 continued to appear and represent the accused no. 2 company. He never pointed out that the proceedings against the said accused no. 2 company already stood dropped. For that matter, even charge/notice was framed against all the accused persons (including accused no. 2 company) on 05.10.2005. The matter was at the stage of PE when the court amended the charge on 27.03.2010, but again, even the amended charge (notice) was framed against all the accused persons (including accused no. 2 company the proceedings against which already stood dropped). Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Sh. Murari Lal Mittal on 15 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/163290650/ 2 5. Be that as it may, after dropping the proceedings against accused no. 2 on 11.02.2004, the matter was listed for further proceedings against accused no. 1 and 3. Apparently, the matter was summons triable in nature being violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act as punishable under section 7/16(ia)(a) of the PFA Act. But instead of framing a notice under section 251 CrPC, two witnesses were examined on 15.02.2005 purportedly under pre-charge stage, despite the fact that there was no order of the court to summon any witness or to list the matter for PE. 6. The complainant examined PW-1 Sh. S. C. Tyagi (SDM/LHA) and PW-2 FI Ranjeet Singh in such pre-charge stage. Based on their deposition, vide order dated 05.10.2005, charge was framed against all the accused persons for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. Subsequently, the witnesses already examined in pre-charge stage were recalled for further cross examination in post charge stage and additionally, the complainant examined PW-3 FI S. B. Sharma in post charge evidence. It is also to be noted that in the meanwhile, on 27.03.2010, the charge was amended by the court and such amended charge was framed against all the accused persons, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. They also chose not to recall any witness already examined for further cross- examination post such amendment in the charge. 7. PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings. All these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 09.08.2002 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 3 polythene pouches of 500 ml each of vanaspati, dividing it in three parts and putting in separate jars, fastening, sealing, marking the sample jars, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses. They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW- 1/A, notice Ex. PW-1/B, Notice under section 14A Ex. PW-1/C, Panchnama Ex. PW-1/D, PA Receipt Ex. PW-2/A and LHA receipt Ex. PW-1/E. PA report Ex. PW-1/F was received and investigation was carried out by PW-2 who sent letter Ex. PW-1/G to the STO and recorded the statement of the vendor Ex. PW-2/B. After completion of investigation, sanction Ex. PW-1/H was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex. PW-1/J was filed in the court by the FI PW-2. A copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-1/K was sent to the accused persons vide postal receipt Ex. PW-1/L. These witnesses were duly cross- examined by Ld. Defence Counsel wherein they denied that the sampling method was not proper or that the accused persons had been falsely implicated or that representative samples were not taken. 8. Statements of the accused persons under section 313 CrPC were recorded on 02.05.2011 wherein they denied the allegations and pleaded innocence. Accused no. 1 claimed that he had purchased the commodity from accused no. 2 and had sold it in same condition as was purchased. Accused no. 2 and 3 on the other hand, disputed the PA and CFL reports on the ground of variation between the two. They however did not lead evidence in defence.
texts.arguments: 9. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused persons beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused persons have not been able to rebut the findings in the CFL report dated Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Sh. Murari Lal Mittal on 15 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/163290650/ 3 17.03.2003 which as per section 13(3) of PFA Act is final and conclusive. It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony. 10. On the other hand, the respective Ld. Defence Counsel have submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various contradictions and missing links in the testimony of witnesses. Ld. Counsel have strongly contended that there is variation in the reports as given by PA and CFL, which leads to conclusion that the two samples were not representative and therefore, conviction cannot be based solely on the basis of the CFL report. They have relied upon the various judgements in his support. It is now argued that when the accused no. 2 company itself has been discharged, its nominee accused no. 3 could be prosecuted under vicarious liability. However, the law has been now settled by the authoritative judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India titled as Aneeta Hada v. Godfather Travels and Travels Pvt. Ltd. [(2012) 5 SCC 661]. In the said precedent, which pertains to the interpretation of section 141 of the Negotiable Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Sh. Murari Lal Mittal on 15 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/163290650/ 4 Instruments Act (NI Act), Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has held that commission of offence by the company is an express condition precedent to attract the vicarious liability of other persons and therefore, it is absolutely clear that only when a company can be prosecuted that the persons mentioned in other categories could be held vicariously liable for the offence committed by the company. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India overruled the previous judgements titled as Sheoratan Agarwal v. State of Madhya Pradash [(1984) 4 SCC 352] and Anil Hada v. Indian Acrylic Ltd. [(2000) 1 SCC 1] and reiterated the law as laid down in State of Madras v. C.V. Parekh [(1970) 3 SCC 491]. Upon going through the law so laid down, it is clear that the prime liability is on the company and it is only when the court comes to conclusion that an offence has been committed by a company that it can proceed to attribute vicarious liability to other persons who are proved to be in charge of or responsible to the company for its affairs. If a nominee has been appointed by a company, he shall be deemed to be so responsible or in charge. Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be. 22. In Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738], it has been authoritatively laid down that the legal impact of a certificate of the Director of CFL is three fold: (a) it annuls or replaces the report of the PA, (b) it gains finality regarding the quality and standard of the food article involved in the case and (c) it becomes irrefutable so far as the facts stated therein are concerned. 23. In Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100], it was observed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi that "It has repeatedly been held by the supreme court that the certificate of the Director supersedes the report of the public analyst and is to be treated as conclusive evidence of its contents. For all purposes the report of the public analyst is replaced by the certificate of the Director.... In this regard, the defence strongly relies upon the judgement titled as Kanshi Nath v. State [2005(2) FAC 219], informing that the said ruling has been constantly followed by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in State v. Ramesh Chand [2010 (2) JCC 1250], Food Inspector v. Parvinder Malik [2014(2) FAC 306], State v. Vinod Kumar Gupta [2010(2) JCC 957], State v. Virender Kohli [2014(2) FAC 223], State v. Kamal Aggarwal [2014(2) FAC 183], State v. Vidya Gupta [2014(1) FAC 291], State v. Dinesh Goswami [2014(1) FAC 302], State v. Mahabir [2014(1) FAC 286], State v. Santosh Sharma [2014(1) FAC 296], Raja Ram Seth & Sons v. Delhi Administration Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1) Sh. Murari Lal Mittal on 15 November, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/163290650/ 6 [2012(2) FAC 523], State v. Sunil Dutt [2011(4) JCC 2377] and State v. Rama Rattan Malhotra [2012(2) FAC 398]. It is submitted that comparison of the two reports would show that there are substantive variations which would show that the sample was not representative. 26. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Kashi Nath's case (supra), was dealing with a situation where there were certain variations in the reports of PA and CFL while analysing a sample of 'dhania powder'. Hon'ble Court considered the ratio in MCD v. Bishan Sarup [ILR 1970 (1) Delhi 518] and held that it would still be open for the accused to establish that the sample tested was not a representative one, and if the variation in the two reports is substantial enough, then the PA report can certainly be looked into to establish this variation. 27. Though the CFL report is final and conclusive as to the results therein, yet it can still be looked into to ascertain if the samples were representative or not. Reliance can be placed on the judgements titled as National Diary Development Board v. State of Haryana [1997(I) PFA Cases 95] and Nebh Raj v. State [Crl. Appeal No. 113/1975, Supreme Court of India, dated 24.10.1980].
